stem: A bucket sends every ObjectCreated event under the uploads/ prefix to an SQS queue used by a thumbnail service, and that destination must stay exactly as it is. A malware scanner and an audit pipeline now need the same events, and the scanner only wants objects larger than 100 MB. Adding a second notification for the same prefix fails because the configuration overlaps. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST effort?

choices.text: Add a second notification for the uploads/ prefix with a .bin suffix for the scanner, and a third with a .csv suffix for the audit pipeline
Replace the queue destination with an SNS topic, subscribe the thumbnail queue plus the two new consumers, and add a size filter for the scanner
Turn on Amazon EventBridge notifications for the bucket, and create two rules for the new consumers, one with a numeric filter on object size
Have the thumbnail service forward each message it receives to the scanner and the audit pipeline after it finishes creating the thumbnail

stem: An Auto Scaling group runs web instances behind an Application Load Balancer. When the application process crashes, the ALB marks the instance unhealthy, but the instance keeps running for hours and capacity stays reduced. New instances need about 4 minutes after launch before the application answers health checks. The team wants failed instances replaced automatically without new instances being killed during startup. What should the team configure?

choices.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, and set the health check grace period to 0 seconds to act at once
Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, and set the health check grace period to about 300 seconds
Add a CloudWatch alarm on each instance's StatusCheckFailed metric with an EC2 reboot action, so crashed instances are restarted
Lower the target group's health check interval to 5 seconds and the unhealthy threshold to 2, so the ALB detects failures faster

stem: An Aurora MySQL cluster has a db.r6g.4xlarge writer in AZ-a, a db.r6g.large reporting replica in AZ-b with promotion tier 0, and a db.r6g.4xlarge replica in AZ-c with promotion tier 1. The application uses the cluster endpoint. In a failover test the small reporting replica became the writer and write latency spiked. The reporting replica must stay, and no instance may be resized. What should be changed?

choices.text: Set the db.r6g.4xlarge replica in AZ-c to promotion tier 0 and the reporting replica to promotion tier 15, so failover prefers the large replica
Modify the reporting replica to db.r6g.4xlarge, so whichever replica Aurora promotes during a failover has the same capacity as the writer
Delete the reporting replica and send reporting queries to the reader endpoint, so the large replica in AZ-c is the only failover target
Point the application at the reader endpoint for writes during a failover, so the remaining large replica serves the writes until the old writer returns

stem: A company runs an Aurora MySQL global database with the primary cluster in us-east-1 and a secondary cluster in eu-west-1 that serves European readers. The European application now needs to save user preferences, a few writes per minute. The team does not want to manage a second database connection to us-east-1 or build cross-Region networking, and it accepts extra write latency. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.text: Store preferences in a DynamoDB global table with replicas in both Regions, and leave the Aurora global database for the relational data
Peer the two VPCs and have the European application open a second connection to the us-east-1 cluster endpoint for preference writes
Promote the eu-west-1 secondary cluster to a standalone cluster, so the European application can write to its own Regional writer endpoint
Enable write forwarding on the eu-west-1 secondary cluster, so writes sent there are forwarded to the primary and replicated back

stem: An RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance in eu-central-1 holds order data. For a Regional outage, the company needs to restore the database in eu-west-1 to any point in the last 7 days, accepts a recovery time of several hours, and wants the lowest ongoing cost, with no database instance running in eu-west-1 before a disaster. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.text: Create an AWS Backup plan with a daily snapshot copied to eu-west-1 and kept for 7 days, and restore the latest copy during a disaster
Create a cross-Region read replica in eu-west-1, and promote it to a standalone DB instance when the primary Region becomes unavailable
Enable cross-Region automated backup replication to eu-west-1 with 7-day retention, and do a point-in-time restore from it when needed
Convert the database to a Multi-AZ DB cluster with two readable standbys, so it can fail over between Availability Zones within seconds

stem: Route 53 latency alias records point to Application Load Balancers in eu-west-1 and us-east-1, both with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes. European users are suddenly routed to us-east-1 although the main application in eu-west-1 is healthy. The eu-west-1 ALB also has a second target group for a retired reporting service whose stopped instances are still registered. Regional failover must keep working. What should the team do?

choices.text: Lower the TTL of the latency alias records to 10 seconds, so that resolvers in Europe pick up the healthy eu-west-1 answer much faster
Associate a Route 53 health check on the main application's URL with the eu-west-1 record, in addition to Evaluate Target Health
Set Evaluate Target Health to No on the eu-west-1 latency alias record, so Route 53 always answers with that Region regardless of ALB health
Remove the listener rule that forwards to the retired target group and delete that group, so only the main application's group is evaluated

stem: A company runs a web application in us-east-1 with EC2 Auto Scaling and an Aurora database. For a Regional outage, the DR Region must be able to take traffic immediately at reduced capacity, without first deploying or starting application servers, and then scale up. In normal operation only us-east-1 may serve users, and DR running costs must be as low as possible within these rules. Which strategy fits?

choices.text: Warm standby: run a scaled-down but working copy of the stack in the DR Region with an Aurora secondary cluster, and scale it up on failover
Multi-site active/active: serve users from both Regions all the time with full capacity, using latency routing and Aurora write forwarding
Hot standby: run full production capacity in the DR Region with an Aurora secondary cluster, and route traffic there only after a failover decision
Pilot light: keep an Aurora secondary cluster in the DR Region and deploy application servers from templates only when failover is invoked

stem: A web application in one Region must keep running with no manual action and no lost user sessions if any one Availability Zone fails. It uses EC2 web servers, a MySQL database, and an in-memory session store. The team accepts brief failover pauses of under a minute but no data loss for committed database transactions. Which THREE design choices meet these requirements? (Select THREE)

choices.text: Store sessions in an ElastiCache for Memcached cluster with nodes spread across three AZs, so each AZ holds its own share of the session data in memory
Store sessions in an ElastiCache for Valkey replication group with Multi-AZ enabled and a replica in a different AZ from the primary node
Keep uploaded files on an io2 EBS volume with Multi-Attach enabled across the web instances, so every web server reads the same files
Add an RDS for MySQL read replica in a second AZ, and have the on-call engineer promote it to be the new primary whenever the primary's AZ fails
Run web servers in an Auto Scaling group across three AZs behind an ALB, with ELB health checks and capacity to serve peak from two AZs
Run the database as an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, which keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over automatically

stem: A media company stores user uploads in S3 buckets in us-east-1 and us-west-2 and runs its application in both Regions. In normal operation all reads and writes must go to us-east-1. During a Regional problem, operators must move all S3 traffic to us-west-2 within minutes, with no application code or configuration change, and the buckets must stay in sync after failback. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.text: Use an S3 Multi-Region Access Point in an active-passive configuration with failover controls, and enable one-way replication from us-east-1 to us-west-2
Use an S3 Multi-Region Access Point in an active-passive configuration with failover controls, and enable two-way Cross-Region Replication between the buckets
Keep a bucket name per Region in the application's configuration, and have operators change the setting and redeploy the application during an outage
Use an S3 Multi-Region Access Point in an active-active configuration, and enable two-way Cross-Region Replication so either Region's bucket can serve requests

stem: A trading firm runs a self-managed PostgreSQL database on a Nitro-based EC2 instance. The data volume needs about 60,000 IOPS of 16 KiB random I/O, and the firm's latency budget requires an average I/O latency under 500 microseconds with as few slow outliers as possible. Data must persist through instance stops, and the database must sit on a single EBS volume to keep snapshots simple. Which storage choice meets the latency requirement?

choices.text: An io2 Block Express volume provisioned with 60,000 IOPS, a type designed for sub-500-microsecond average latency on 16 KiB I/O
A gp3 volume provisioned with 60,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s of throughput, sized at 120 GiB or more to respect the 500 IOPS per GiB ratio
The NVMe instance store volumes of a storage-optimized instance, combined into one device and mounted as the database data directory
Four gp3 volumes of 15,000 IOPS each, striped together with RAID 0 in the operating system so that their IOPS add up on one device

stem: A media company's render farm mounts a 200 GiB Amazon EFS file system that uses Bursting throughput. For about 20 hours every day the farm reads and writes a steady 150 MiB/s, and CloudWatch shows BurstCreditBalance falling to zero by mid-morning, after which jobs crawl. The data set will not grow, and the team refuses to store padding files. Following AWS guidance for a known, steady requirement, which change restores throughput at the LOWEST cost?

choices.text: Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that EFS scales throughput automatically and bills for each gigabyte of data and metadata read or written
Write about 3 TiB of placeholder data into EFS Standard storage, so the Bursting baseline, which grows with stored data, rises to 150 MiB/s
Recreate the file system in the Max I/O performance mode, which is designed for highly parallel workloads with many clients reading at once
Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput at 150 MiB/s, which delivers that rate regardless of the stored data size or burst credit balance

stem: A geospatial analytics service on a network-optimized EC2 instance downloads 40 GB satellite images from an S3 bucket in the same Region, and each object is fetched with a single GET request. A download takes several minutes while the instance's network interface stays below 15 percent use. The upload process and object key layout belong to another team and cannot change, and the data must not be copied elsewhere. Which change shortens the downloads the MOST?

choices.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and download through the accelerate endpoint, which routes requests over CloudFront edge locations to the bucket
Have the keys spread across many hashed prefixes, so that the bucket supports more GET requests per second for each partitioned prefix
Split each download into many concurrent byte-range GET requests over separate connections, for example with the SDK transfer manager
Copy the images into an S3 Express One Zone directory bucket in the instance's Availability Zone and read them from there with single requests

stem: An order-import Lambda function is triggered by an SQS standard queue whose redrive policy sends messages to a dead-letter queue after three receives. During sales Lambda scales to hundreds of concurrent invocations, and the Aurora writer, which handles about 50 concurrent writes well, slows sharply. The team set reserved concurrency to 50, but valid messages then reached the DLQ. Messages must not be retried because of throttling, and other functions must keep their concurrency. What should the team do?

choices.text: Remove the reserved concurrency and set maximum concurrency to 50 on the SQS event source mapping, so Lambda reads fewer batches instead of throttling
Keep reserved concurrency at 50 and raise maxReceiveCount on the redrive policy to 20, so throttled messages get more attempts before reaching the DLQ
Configure provisioned concurrency of 50 on the function alias, so that only 50 pre-initialized execution environments can process messages from the queue
Raise the event source mapping batch size to 10,000 messages with a batching window, so that each invocation writes many more orders to Aurora

stem: A booking API runs on an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Every weekday at 08:00, traffic triples within minutes, and smaller unplanned spikes occur during the day. Each new instance needs about seven minutes to download a large reference data set to its EBS volume before it passes health checks, so users see errors during scale-out. The company wants fast scale-out for both kinds of surge without paying for idle running instances. Which TWO actions should the solutions architect take? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Shorten the health check grace period to 60 seconds, so that new instances join the load balancer before the data download completes
Add a warm pool that keeps instances in the Running state, so pre-initialized instances can join the group without any boot delay
Add a predictive scaling policy, so the group forecasts the weekday surge from its history and launches capacity ahead of 08:00
Add a scheduled action that raises the minimum capacity to the 08:00 peak for the whole business day, so enough instances always run
Add a warm pool that keeps instances Stopped, with a lifecycle hook so that each one finishes the download before it is stopped

stem: A company is moving a 60-node Apache Cassandra cluster to EC2 in one Region with three Availability Zones, placing 20 nodes in each zone. A single rack failure inside a zone must never take out more than one replica of the same data, so Cassandra needs to know which rack each node is on. All three zones must be used, and node-to-node network performance only needs to be normal for the zone. Which placement design fits?

choices.text: A cluster placement group in each Availability Zone, so that the 20 nodes in each zone share a low-latency, high-bandwidth network segment
A single partition placement group in one Availability Zone with seven partitions, mapping each partition to a Cassandra rack for replica placement
A spread placement group across the three Availability Zones, so that every one of the 60 nodes runs on its own distinct rack with separate power
A partition placement group with partitions in each Availability Zone, mapping each partition to a Cassandra rack by its partition number

stem: A mobile backend runs on Lambda functions with 128 MB of memory. Tracing shows three problems: requests right after the 09:00 traffic jump spend 3 seconds in initialization, a CPU-bound scoring step takes 900 ms, and every invocation spends 150 ms opening a new TLS connection to an RDS for MySQL database. The company wants lower p99 latency and accepts a higher Lambda bill. Which THREE changes address the observed problems? (Select THREE)

choices.text: Configure reserved concurrency equal to the 09:00 peak, so that the function always has enough execution environments set aside for it alone
Add an RDS Proxy in front of the database and open the connection outside the handler, so that warm environments reuse pooled connections
Increase the function timeout from 3 seconds to 30 seconds, so that slow invocations during initialization finish instead of failing with a timeout
Increase ephemeral storage in /tmp from 512 MB to 10 GB, so the function can keep scoring results on local disk between invocations
Raise the memory setting to about 1,769 MB or more, because Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to the configured memory
Configure provisioned concurrency on the function alias, scheduled with Application Auto Scaling to rise before 09:00 each day

stem: A ticketing site added a three-node DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of its seat-map table, but read latency and consumed read capacity did not change at all. Investigation shows that every GetItem call sets ConsistentRead to true, a setting copied from an old code sample. Product owners confirm that seat maps may be up to two seconds stale. What should the team do to get the expected benefit from DAX?

choices.text: Change the GetItem calls to eventually consistent reads, so that DAX can answer them from its item cache instead of DynamoDB
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB serves the strongly consistent reads behind DAX with no capacity planning
Raise the item cache TTL in the DAX parameter group from 5 minutes to 1 hour, so that cached seat maps stay in memory much longer
Scale the DAX cluster to a larger node type and add nodes, so that the item cache can hold the entire seat-map table in memory at once

stem: A gaming company keeps player profiles in Aurora MySQL and wants a real-time global leaderboard that returns the top 100 players in under a millisecond. Scores change thousands of times per second, and the ranking must always reflect the latest scores. If a cache node fails, the leaderboard must fail over automatically within the Region without being rebuilt from the database. Which design meets these requirements?

choices.text: Aurora Replicas with an index on the score column, reading the top 100 through the reader endpoint with ORDER BY and LIMIT clauses
ElastiCache for Valkey with Multi-AZ replicas and automatic failover, keeping scores in a sorted set read with a range command
A DynamoDB Accelerator cluster placed in front of the Aurora MySQL tables, caching the result of the top-100 query for one second at a time
ElastiCache for Memcached with several nodes, storing each player's score under its own key and computing the top 100 in the application

stem: An Aurora PostgreSQL cluster has a writer and four db.r6g.large replicas serving a web application through the reader endpoint. Analysts need long-running reports, so two db.r6g.4xlarge replicas were added. Since then, some web reads land on the large replicas and some reports land on the small ones, making web latency unpredictable. Web reads must never share instances with reports, and all instances must stay in this cluster. What should the solutions architect do?

choices.text: Point the reporting tool at the reader endpoint and give the two large replicas failover priority tier 15, so that the reader endpoint avoids sending them traffic
Turn on Aurora Auto Scaling for replicas with a 60 percent CPU target, so that the reader endpoint always has spare capacity for both workloads
Move the reports to a separate Aurora cluster created as a clone every night, and point the reporting tool at that cluster's own reader endpoint
Create one custom endpoint for the two large replicas and another for the four small ones, and point reports and web reads at their own endpoints

stem: A streaming company packages video segments just in time on servers in its own data center, behind a CloudFront distribution with a well-tuned cache policy. Viewers are spread across five continents. When a popular segment is first requested, the packagers receive near-simultaneous requests for it from many regional edge caches, which overloads them. Segments must keep their current short TTL. Which change reduces the load on the origin the MOST?

choices.text: Add a second origin in an origin group that fails over on 5xx errors, so that CloudFront retries overloaded requests against a standby packager
Put an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator in front of the data center servers, so that CloudFront reaches the origin over the AWS global network
Enable Origin Shield in the AWS Region with the lowest latency to the data center, so every cache layer fetches through one extra caching layer
Increase the default and maximum TTL in the cache policy to 24 hours, so that every regional edge cache keeps each segment much longer

stem: A company runs a stateful multiplayer lobby service on Network Load Balancers in two Regions behind an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator. Each game client opens several TCP connections from different source ports, and lobby state lives only in memory on the endpoint that first served the player. Players are dropped from lobbies when a later connection lands on another endpoint. The static anycast IP addresses must not change. What should the solutions architect configure?

choices.text: Enable client IP address preservation on the Network Load Balancer endpoints, so that the lobby service sees each player's real address on every connection
Set the traffic dial of both endpoint groups to 100 percent with equal endpoint weights, so that each Region receives a predictable share of connections
Set the listener's client affinity to Source IP, so that Global Accelerator hashes on source and destination IP and keeps a player on one endpoint
Replace the accelerator with a CloudFront distribution that uses both Network Load Balancers as origins with a cache policy that forwards all headers

stem: A company copies database backups from EC2 instances in us-east-1 to instances in eu-west-1 over an inter-Region VPC peering connection. All instances use a 9001-byte MTU, which gives excellent throughput inside each VPC. Small replication messages succeed, but large transfers stall. The subnets' network ACLs deny all ICMP traffic. Jumbo frames must remain enabled for traffic inside each VPC. What should the solutions architect do?

choices.text: Replace the peering connection with peered transit gateways and keep the 9001-byte MTU, since transit gateways route traffic between the two Regions
Set the MTU of every instance in both VPCs to 1,500 bytes, so that all packets fit through the peering connection without being fragmented
Launch the instances in each Region into a cluster placement group, so that packets take the shortest network path and are not fragmented
Allow inbound ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages (type 3, code 4) in the network ACLs and security groups, so Path MTU Discovery works

stem: A startup launches a smart-meter platform next month. Write traffic into its Kinesis data stream will grow from about 2 MB/s to an unknown peak over several weeks, with daily swings that are hard to forecast. One consumer reads with GetRecords and must be able to replay the last 24 hours. Nobody on the team can monitor shard metrics or run resharding, and the company will not pay for capacity sized to a guessed peak. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: A provisioned-mode stream sized at 50 shards for an estimated peak, with a CloudWatch alarm that notifies the team when write throughput exceeds 80 percent
An on-demand mode stream that adds capacity as new write peaks appear, accommodating up to double the previous 30-day peak, billed per GB
An Amazon SQS standard queue in place of the stream, because it scales to a nearly unlimited message rate without any capacity settings
A provisioned-mode stream with a Lambda function that calls UpdateShardCount from CloudWatch alarms, scaling shards up and down as traffic changes

stem: A payments platform in us-east-1 sends ledger events to an SQS FIFO queue with one SendMessage call per event, using the same MessageGroupId for every event. Sends are throttled at about 300 per second, but the business now needs about 6,000 events per second. Ordering matters only among events for the same account, and the platform must keep FIFO exactly-once processing on a single queue. Which TWO changes should the solutions architect make? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Set MessageGroupId to the account ID on each event, so ordering holds per account while messages spread across many groups and partitions
Spread events across 20 FIFO queues chosen by a hash of the account ID, each with its own consumer fleet and its own dead-letter queue
Replace the FIFO queue with an SQS standard queue and deduplicate in the consumer, because standard queues allow a nearly unlimited API call rate
Batch sends with SendMessageBatch in groups of 10 while keeping the single message group ID, which lifts the queue to 3,000 messages per second
Enable high throughput mode on the FIFO queue, which raises the transaction quota for each API action far beyond 300 per second in this Region

stem: A logistics company runs Apache Kafka on its own servers. Fifty producer and consumer applications use the Kafka client libraries, Kafka Streams, and Kafka Connect connectors. The company must move to AWS within one quarter without changing any application code, and its small platform team does not want to install, patch, or replace broker servers. Which service should the solutions architect choose for the streaming layer?

choices.text: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ, using durable queues and exchanges in place of Kafka topics and treating consumer groups as competing consumers
Apache Kafka installed on EC2 instances across three Availability Zones with EBS volumes, using the same broker settings as the current servers
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, rewriting the producers with the Kinesis Producer Library and the consumers with the Kinesis Client Library
Amazon MSK, which runs open-source Apache Kafka with AWS operating the brokers, so existing clients, Streams apps, and connectors keep working

stem: A company is moving a reporting database from its data center to a 2 TiB EBS volume on a Nitro-based EC2 instance. Load tests show it needs a sustained 40,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s of throughput, and single-digit-millisecond latency is acceptable. The database runs on one volume and does not use Multi-Attach. Which volume configuration meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

choices.text: An io2 Block Express volume with 40,000 provisioned IOPS, giving the throughput with sub-millisecond latency and higher volume durability
A Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume, designed for large sequential workloads and priced much lower per GiB than SSD volumes
A gp3 volume with 40,000 provisioned IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s of throughput, paying only for performance above the included baseline
A gp2 volume sized at 14 TiB, so that its baseline of 3 IOPS per GiB of size reaches the 40,000 IOPS that the workload needs

stem: An insurer must keep 900 TB of closed claim files for 10 years. The files are almost never read, but when a regulator requests a set of files, they must be available within 24 hours of the request. The company wants the lowest storage cost and accepts per-request retrieval fees. Files are written to S3 once and never modified. Which approach meets these requirements?

choices.text: Store the files in S3 Glacier Deep Archive and restore requested files with the Standard retrieval option, which usually finishes within 12 hours
Store the files in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, so that any requested file can be read at once with a GET request and no restore step
Store the files in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and restore requested files with free Bulk retrievals, which usually finish within 5 to 12 hours
Store the files in S3 Glacier Deep Archive and restore requested files with the Bulk retrieval option, the lowest-cost way to retrieve archived data

stem: A manufacturer takes a monthly EBS snapshot of each of 300 production volumes through an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy and must keep every monthly snapshot for seven years. The three newest snapshots are sometimes restored within an hour for testing; older ones have never been restored, and auditors accept up to three days to get one back. Which change reduces snapshot storage cost the MOST while keeping these rules?

choices.text: Keep all snapshots in the standard tier, but after three months delete every monthly snapshot except the January one, keeping one snapshot per year
Add an archiving rule to the monthly schedule in the Data Lifecycle Manager policy, moving each snapshot to the archive tier after three months
Enable fast snapshot restore on every monthly snapshot older than three months, so that any audit restore can complete at once instead of within three days
Add an archiving rule that moves every snapshot to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier as soon as it is created, so each one spends seven years in the archive tier

stem: A company opted in to AWS Compute Optimizer for 400 EC2 instances that run Java services. It recommends downsizing many memory-heavy r-family instances, but engineers distrust the advice: the console shows no memory data for these instances, and the busiest days are month-end runs that fall outside the default lookback period. The company wants recommendations it can trust before resizing anything. Which TWO actions should the solutions architect take? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Activate the enhanced infrastructure metrics preference, so that Compute Optimizer analyzes up to 93 days of metrics instead of 14
Base the resizing on Cost Explorer cost and usage graphs for the past month, filtered by instance type, to find instances with low spend
Turn on EC2 detailed monitoring for the instances, so that one-minute CPU and network metrics give Compute Optimizer finer data to analyze
Stream the instances' CloudWatch metrics to Amazon Data Firehose with a metric stream, so that Compute Optimizer receives the month-end data continuously
Install the CloudWatch agent on the instances to publish memory utilization, so Compute Optimizer includes memory in its analysis

stem: A company runs a steady fleet of m6i instances in one Region around the clock and wants to make a three-year commitment for a discount. Within nine months it will move the whole fleet to Graviton-based m7g instances, and some services may later move to AWS Fargate. The finance team will not manage exchanges or modifications of reservations. Which purchase keeps a commitment discount applying through these changes?

choices.text: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the m6i family in the Region, which offers the deepest Savings Plans discount for a committed instance family
Convertible Reserved Instances for m6i, exchanged for m7g Convertible Reserved Instances after each part of the fleet completes its migration
A Compute Savings Plan for the steady hourly spend, which applies across instance families, sizes, Regions, and Fargate without any exchanges
Standard Reserved Instances for m6i with regional scope, using instance size flexibility to cover the different instance sizes in the fleet

stem: A company must keep capacity for 30 instances available in one specific Availability Zone for a year to meet a contractual guarantee. The instances run continuously, and the team expects to switch between m7i and m7g instance types during the year. The company wants guaranteed capacity in that zone and the largest discount that still applies after the instance type change. Which approach meets these requirements?

choices.text: Buy zonal Reserved Instances for m7i in the zone, which reserve capacity there and give a discount for that instance type and size only
Create On-Demand Capacity Reservations in the zone and buy a Compute Savings Plan, whose discount also applies to that capacity
Create On-Demand Capacity Reservations in the zone without any other purchase, keeping the whole fleet at On-Demand rates for the year
Buy a Compute Savings Plan for the hourly spend and rely on it to hold capacity for the fleet in the zone during periods of high demand

stem: A retailer reviews its EC2 costs. Its web tier runs 12 On-Demand instances around the clock, rising to 30 during business hours, and must never lose capacity to interruptions. A nightly report job checkpoints its progress and has a six-hour window, so it can rerun if needed. Twenty development instances are used only during weekday office hours. Which THREE actions reduce cost while meeting these requirements? (Select THREE)

choices.text: Buy a Savings Plan sized to the daytime peak of 30 instances, so that every web instance is covered by the discounted rate at all hours
Move the development instances to Dedicated Hosts, so that the company pays one hourly host price instead of twenty instance prices
Run the web tier entirely on Spot Instances with a capacity-optimized strategy, relying on Auto Scaling to replace interrupted instances
Stop the development instances outside office hours on a schedule, since a stopped instance bills for its EBS volumes but not for compute
Buy a Savings Plan sized to the around-the-clock baseline of 12 instances and keep the daytime extra capacity on On-Demand pricing
Run the nightly report job on Spot Instances across several instance types using the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy

stem: A company runs an RDS for PostgreSQL database on a db.r6i.xlarge Single-AZ instance and wants to buy a three-year reserved DB instance today. In about four months it will convert the database to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and scale it to db.r6i.2xlarge, staying on the r6i class in the same Region. It wants the discount to cover the database without paying for unused reservations in the meantime. What should it buy?

choices.text: A Compute Savings Plan sized to the database's hourly On-Demand cost, because it applies regardless of instance family, size, or AWS Region
A reserved DB instance for db.r7g.xlarge Single-AZ, because newer Graviton classes give a lower hourly rate for the same normalized size
A db.r6i.xlarge Single-AZ reservation now and more r6i reservations after the change, since size flexibility spans sizes and deployments
A reserved DB instance for db.r6i.2xlarge Multi-AZ today, so that the final configuration is fully covered from the very first day of the term

stem: A DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode stores 400 million session items. Each night a Lambda function scans the table and deletes items older than 30 days, consuming so many write capacity units that the table is scaled up for two hours. Expired items may remain for a few days before deletion, but every deleted session must be archived to S3 for compliance. Which TWO changes meet the requirements at the LOWEST cost? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Keep the nightly delete job but switch the table to on-demand capacity mode, so the burst of deletes is billed per request instead of by scaled capacity
Enable Time to Live on an expiry attribute set to 30 days after creation, because DynamoDB deletes expired items without using write throughput
Change the table class to DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access, which lowers storage costs for tables that keep many rarely read items
Run a daily full export of the table to S3, so that an archive copy of every session exists in S3 before the delete job removes it
Enable DynamoDB Streams and use a Lambda function that writes to S3 the records whose userIdentity principal is dynamodb.amazonaws.com

stem: A QA department needs five test copies of a 6 TB Aurora MySQL production cluster, refreshed every Monday. Each copy changes less than 2 percent of the data during its week, testers need full read and write access, and copies must be ready within an hour of the refresh starting. The company wants to keep the extra storage cost of the test copies as low as possible. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Add five Aurora Replicas to the production cluster and give each test team the instance endpoint of one replica for its testing during the week
Use AWS DMS full load plus ongoing replication into five separate Aurora clusters, keeping every test copy continuously in step with production
Restore the latest automated snapshot into five new clusters each Monday, giving every test team an independent full copy of the 6 TB volume
Create five Aurora clones of the production cluster each Monday, which share unchanged pages copy-on-write and store only changes

stem: A company routes all outbound traffic from 40 spoke VPCs through a transit gateway to NAT gateways in a central egress VPC in the same Region. Most of this traffic is reads from S3 buckets in that Region. The team added an S3 gateway endpoint to the egress VPC, but NAT gateway and transit gateway data processing charges did not drop. Which change reduces these charges the MOST?

choices.text: Create an S3 gateway endpoint in each spoke VPC and associate it with the spoke route tables, so S3 traffic skips both transit gateway and NAT
Add routes on the transit gateway route tables that send the S3 prefix list to the egress VPC attachment, so traffic reaches the gateway endpoint there
Deploy a NAT gateway in each spoke VPC, so that S3 traffic leaves directly from each spoke without crossing the transit gateway at all
Create an S3 interface endpoint in the egress VPC and resolve its DNS names from the spoke VPCs, so S3 traffic no longer passes through NAT

stem: An application VPC and a search-cluster VPC in the same Region exchange about 300 TB a month through the company's transit gateway, which also connects 25 other VPCs. The instances that talk to each other are in the same Availability Zones in both VPCs. Data processing charges for this one pair now dominate the transit gateway bill. Which change reduces cost the MOST without changing how the other VPCs connect?

choices.text: Attach both VPCs to a second, dedicated transit gateway, so that their traffic no longer shares processing with the 25 other VPC attachments
Enable appliance mode on both transit gateway VPC attachments, so that traffic between the pair stays in one Availability Zone and avoids cross-AZ charges
Create a VPC peering connection between the two VPCs and add routes for each other's CIDR blocks, which are more specific than the transit gateway routes
Expose the search cluster through an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer, with an interface endpoint in the application VPC

stem: An application runs on 120 EC2 instances in public subnets behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer, and each instance has an auto-assigned public IPv4 address. The instances receive traffic only from the load balancer and download packages only from an S3 bucket in the same Region. The VPC has no IPv6 CIDR block, and adding IPv6 is out of scope. Which change removes the public IPv4 charges at the LOWEST cost?

choices.text: Replace the auto-assigned addresses with Elastic IP addresses allocated to the account, so that each instance keeps a fixed address for the long term
Move the instances to private subnets without public IPv4 addresses and add an S3 gateway endpoint for package downloads, keeping the ALB public
Add an egress-only internet gateway, send the instances' outbound traffic through it, and then remove the public IPv4 addresses from the instances
Move the instances to private subnets and send their outbound traffic through a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone to reach Amazon S3

stem: A Spark cluster in eu-west-1 reads the same 50 TB reference dataset about ten times a month from an S3 bucket in us-east-1 through a NAT gateway in its private subnets. The dataset changes by only a few gigabytes each day. The team created an S3 gateway endpoint in the eu-west-1 VPC, but NAT charges did not change. Which approach reduces data transfer and NAT charges the MOST?

choices.text: Copy the dataset once to an eu-west-1 bucket with S3 Batch Replication, keep it current with Cross-Region Replication, and read it locally
Add the us-east-1 bucket's ARN to the gateway endpoint policy in eu-west-1, so that the endpoint carries requests for that bucket instead of the NAT
Create an S3 interface endpoint in a us-east-1 VPC and reach it from the cluster over inter-Region VPC peering, so reads no longer use the NAT gateway
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the us-east-1 bucket and have the cluster read through the accelerate endpoint for faster cross-Region transfers

stem: A security account owns a customer managed KMS key that encrypts the EBS snapshots behind a hardened AMI, and it shares the AMI with a workload account. The key policy already allows the workload account (its account principal) kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt, kms:ReEncrypt*, kms:GenerateDataKey*, kms:DescribeKey, and kms:CreateGrant. An engineer in the workload account launches the AMI manually without problems. However, an Auto Scaling group in the workload account that uses the AMI through a launch template, with the default service-linked role, fails every launch with "Client.InternalError: Client error on launch". The security team will not add individual workload-account roles to its key policy, and every volume must stay encrypted with the security account's key. What should the team do?

choices.text: Copy the AMI into the workload account and re-encrypt its snapshots with the aws/ebs AWS managed key, which the service-linked role can already use
In the workload account, attach an inline policy to the AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling role that allows kms:Decrypt and kms:CreateGrant on the key's ARN
In the security account, add the workload account's AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling role ARN as a principal in the key policy statement that allows kms:CreateGrant
From the workload account, create a KMS grant on the security account's key that names the workload account's AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling role as the grantee principal

stem: A finance bucket's policy has one Deny statement for s3:* on the bucket and its objects, with a NotIpAddress condition on aws:SourceIp that lists the office range 203.0.113.0/24 and 198.51.100.7, the Elastic IP of the VPC's NAT gateway. Reporting instances in private subnets used to reach the bucket through that NAT gateway. To cut NAT data processing charges, the network team added an S3 gateway endpoint, vpce-0a1b2c, to the private route tables. Since then the instances get 403 AccessDenied from the bucket, while office users still succeed. The bucket must stay reachable only from the office range and through this one endpoint, and the endpoint must stay. What should the solutions architect change?

choices.text: Add the VPC's private CIDR 10.40.0.0/16 to the aws:SourceIp values in the Deny statement's NotIpAddress condition, so the instances' addresses match
Attach an endpoint policy to vpce-0a1b2c that allows s3:* on the finance bucket for the reporting role, so the endpoint itself authorizes those requests
Add a separate Allow statement for s3:* with an aws:SourceVpce condition equal to vpce-0a1b2c, so requests through the endpoint are allowed next to the Deny
Add a StringNotEquals condition on aws:SourceVpce with the value vpce-0a1b2c to the same Deny statement, so only requests that fail both tests are denied

stem: A shared-services account stores a database credential in AWS Secrets Manager. The secret is encrypted with the default aws/secretsmanager key and rotated every 30 days by a Lambda function in that account. An application role in a separate workload account must now read the secret at startup. The workload role's identity policy already allows secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret's ARN and kms:Decrypt on every KMS key in the shared-services account, yet its calls fail with AccessDenied. Security rules: the credential must live in exactly one secret so rotation stays in one place, and no principal other than that one workload role may gain access. Which THREE actions together grant the access? (Select THREE)

choices.text: Replicate the secret into the workload account with ReplicateSecretToRegions, so the application role reads a local replica that rotation keeps in sync
Add a statement to the aws/secretsmanager key's policy that allows the workload role's ARN to use kms:Decrypt, so the secret keeps its current key
Add a statement to the new customer managed key's key policy that allows the workload role's ARN to use kms:Decrypt and kms:DescribeKey
Attach a resource-based policy to the secret that allows the workload account's root principal, so the account's administrators can delegate access
Re-encrypt the secret with a new customer managed KMS key in the shared-services account, and give the rotation function's role access to that key
Attach a resource-based policy to the secret that allows the workload role's ARN, and only that ARN, to call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue

stem: A document service on Amazon ECS on Fargate emails each partner a download link to its quarterly report in a private S3 bucket. The task role creates S3 presigned URLs with a 7-day expiration, but partners report 403 responses with an ExpiredToken error when they open a link more than a few hours after the email arrives. Security policy bans long-term IAM user access keys, and the bucket must stay private. Links must work for the full 7 days, and if the signing material ever leaks, the company must be able to stop honoring all outstanding links at once without rotating anything in IAM. What should the solutions architect do?

choices.text: Have the task call AssumeRole on a dedicated signing role with DurationSeconds set to 604,800, and sign the presigned URLs with that session's credentials
Front the bucket with a CloudFront distribution that uses origin access control, and issue CloudFront signed URLs from a trusted key group with a 7-day expiry
Raise the ECS task role's maximum session duration to 12 hours, so the credentials that sign each 7-day presigned URL remain valid long enough for partners
Create a signing IAM user, store its access keys in Secrets Manager with 90-day rotation, and sign the 7-day presigned URLs with those long-term keys

stem: Application instances run Amazon Linux in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer and call a payment provider's HTTPS API through a NAT gateway in a public subnet. The security team replaced the private subnets' network ACL with one that has these rules. Inbound: allow TCP 8080 from the ALB subnets; then deny all. Outbound: allow TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0, allow TCP 1024-65535 to the ALB subnets; then deny all. The public subnets keep the default network ACL. Web pages still load, but every payment call now times out. VPC flow logs on an instance's network interface show 10.0.2.15 to 203.0.113.50, destination port 443, ACCEPT, and 203.0.113.50 to 10.0.2.15, source port 443, destination port 45512, REJECT. What should the team add?

choices.text: An inbound rule in the private subnets' network ACL that allows TCP 32768-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0, placed before the final deny rule
An inbound rule in the instances' security group that allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, so the payment provider's responses can return
An inbound rule in the private subnets' network ACL that allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, placed before the final deny rule
An outbound rule in the private subnets' network ACL that allows TCP 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0, the port range a NAT gateway uses

stem: A company inspects all traffic between spoke VPCs with stateful firewall instances in an inspection VPC attached to a transit gateway. The inspection VPC has one firewall instance per Availability Zone in AZ-a and AZ-b; each transit gateway attachment subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall in the same zone. Spoke VPC 1 has workloads only in AZ-a, and spoke VPC 2 has workloads only in AZ-b. Connections between two instances in the same zone work, but TCP sessions between spoke VPC 1 and spoke VPC 2 fail, and the firewall logs show SYN-ACK packets dropped as out of state. The inspection design must stay as is. What should the network team change?

choices.text: Turn on equal-cost multipath routing support on the transit gateway so return traffic can use either firewall
Enable appliance mode support on the transit gateway attachments of both spoke VPCs
Enable appliance mode support on the transit gateway attachment of the inspection VPC
Add a subnet in AZ-b to spoke VPC 1's transit gateway attachment and a subnet in AZ-a to spoke VPC 2's attachment

stem: A team runs Docker containers in the default bridge network on EC2 instances that it manages itself, without Amazon ECS. Code in the containers uses an AWS SDK and gets credentials from the instance profile through the instance metadata service. To meet a new security baseline, the team updated the launch template to set HttpTokens to required, keeping all other metadata options at their defaults. Agents running directly on the host still work, but SDK calls inside the containers now hang and then fail to find credentials. The baseline requires IMDSv2 only, and the metadata token must not be usable more than one network hop beyond the containers. What should the team change in the launch template?

choices.text: Set HttpPutResponseHopLimit to 2 and keep HttpTokens set to required
Keep the defaults and pass the AWS Region to each container as an environment variable
Enable HttpProtocolIpv6 so containers reach the IPv6 metadata endpoint instead
Set HttpTokens to optional for these instances so containers can use IMDSv1

stem: In a shared account, 40 developers create and update Lambda functions. Each function must run with one of the pre-approved execution roles named app-lambda-*, which trust lambda.amazonaws.com. The account also holds older admin roles that trust both Lambda and EC2; developers must never be able to give a function one of those roles, or hand an app-lambda-* role to any other service. Auditors also want a monthly report of which role each function received and who set it. A first attempt tagged the approved roles approved=true and allowed iam:PassRole only on resources with that tag, but it behaved inconsistently. Which TWO actions meet the requirements? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Allow iam:PassRole on all roles when aws:ResourceTag/approved equals true, adding an iam:PassedToService condition for lambda.amazonaws.com
Build the report from CloudTrail CreateFunction and UpdateFunctionConfiguration events, which record the role passed and the identity that called
Add a condition to each admin role's trust policy that lets lambda.amazonaws.com assume it only when aws:SourceAccount equals this account
Build the report from CloudTrail events whose event name is PassRole and event source is iam.amazonaws.com, filtered to the app-lambda-* roles
Allow iam:PassRole only on arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/app-lambda-*, with an iam:PassedToService condition equal to lambda.amazonaws.com

stem: A retail app uses an Amazon Cognito identity pool in production with guest access turned on, so anonymous visitors can browse the catalog, and with a Cognito user pool as the sign-in provider. The same AWS account also runs a staging identity pool that uses the same user pool. A new IAM role, OrderHistoryReader, must issue temporary credentials only to signed-in users of the production identity pool: never to guests, and never to any user of the staging pool. The role's trust policy names the principal cognito-identity.amazonaws.com and allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Which condition block should the trust policy contain?

choices.text: StringEquals on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud equal to the user pool app client ID, plus ForAnyValue:StringLike on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:amr equal to authenticated
StringEquals on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud equal to the production identity pool ID, plus ForAnyValue:StringLike on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:amr equal to unauthenticated
StringEquals on aws:SourceAccount equal to the company's account ID, plus ForAnyValue:StringLike on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:amr equal to authenticated
StringEquals on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:aud equal to the production identity pool ID, plus ForAnyValue:StringLike on cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:amr equal to authenticated

stem: Account A replicates a bucket to a bucket in account B in another Region. Source objects use SSE-KMS with key KA in account A; the replication rule encrypts replicas with key KB, owned by account B, and SseKmsEncryptedObjects is enabled. Replication worked for months. To cut KMS request costs, both teams then enabled S3 Bucket Keys on both buckets. Since then, new SSE-KMS objects show replication status FAILED, while the few SSE-S3 objects still replicate. The replication role allows kms:Decrypt on KA when kms:EncryptionContext:aws:s3:arn is like arn:aws:s3:::src-bucket/*, and kms:Encrypt on KB when it is like arn:aws:s3:::dst-bucket/*. KB's key policy grants that role kms:Encrypt only. Which TWO changes restore replication while keeping Bucket Keys? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Change the rule's ReplicaKmsKeyID to account B's aws/s3 AWS managed key, which S3 can use for replicas without key policy changes
Change both encryption context conditions in the role policy to the bucket ARNs, arn:aws:s3:::src-bucket and arn:aws:s3:::dst-bucket
Add kms:GenerateDataKey on KA to the role policy, so the role can create a new data key for every object it replicates
Replace s3:GetObjectVersionForReplication with s3:GetObjectVersion in the role policy, so S3 can read each encrypted source version
Allow the replication role kms:Decrypt on KB, both in KB's key policy and in the role's policy, next to the existing kms:Encrypt

stem: A payments platform runs an Aurora PostgreSQL global database with the primary cluster in us-east-1 and one secondary cluster in us-west-2. Auditors now require that an unplanned Regional failover can lose at most 30 seconds of committed transactions. The AuroraGlobalDBRPOLag metric is normally under 1 second but reaches about 45 seconds during the nightly batch load. The business accepts that writes stall briefly during such peaks. However, after a real failover to us-west-2, the new primary must accept writes immediately, long before a replacement secondary exists. How should the team configure the rds.global_db_rpo parameter?

choices.text: Set it to 30 in a custom DB cluster parameter group on the primary cluster, and leave the us-west-2 cluster's parameter group at its default value
Set it to 30 only in the us-west-2 cluster's parameter group, because Aurora measures the RPO lag on the secondary cluster that receives the changes
Set it to 10 in a custom DB cluster parameter group on the primary cluster only, which keeps a 20-second safety margin below the audited limit
Set it to 30 in custom DB cluster parameter groups on both clusters, so the same bound stays enforced as soon as us-west-2 becomes the primary

stem: A wallet service keeps balances in a 400 GB DynamoDB table in us-east-1 with on-demand capacity. The table has a local secondary index that the monthly statement page queries by date, and those queries tolerate slightly stale results. The company now wants active-active writes in us-east-1 and us-east-2 with a recovery point objective of zero. Every strongly consistent read and every conditional write in either Region must see the latest balance. Finance will not pay for a full third copy of the data, and a planned migration window with paused writes is available. Which plan meets these requirements?

choices.text: Add a us-east-2 replica to the existing table in the default eventual consistency mode, and make every balance read in both Regions strongly consistent
Add a us-east-2 replica to the existing table, choose multi-Region strong consistency as the global table's mode, and keep the local secondary index for statements
Create a new, empty table with a GSI in place of the LSI as an MRSC global table with replicas in us-east-1 and us-east-2 plus a witness in us-west-2, then load the data
Create a new, empty table that keeps the LSI as an MRSC global table with replicas only in us-east-1 and us-east-2, then load the data during the window

stem: A publishing system keeps 3 TB of article assets, about 2 million files with none larger than 2 GB, on an Amazon EFS file system in eu-west-1. The DR plan needs a copy in eu-central-1 with an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 2 hours. In a quarterly drill, editors work against eu-central-1 for a day, and everything they create there must end up on the eu-west-1 file system when the drill ends, after which eu-west-1 resumes as the primary. Which THREE steps make up this plan? (Select THREE)

choices.text: To fail back, re-create the original replication configuration from eu-west-1 to eu-central-1, which copies the drill changes back into eu-west-1
Protect the file system with daily AWS Backup jobs that copy recovery points to eu-central-1, and restore the newest copy to a new file system in a drill
To fail over, keep the replication configuration and set replication overwrite protection on the eu-central-1 file system to ENABLED to make it writable
To fail back, disable replication overwrite protection on the eu-west-1 file system, replicate eu-central-1 to it, then re-create the original configuration
To fail over, delete the replication configuration so that the eu-central-1 file system becomes writable, then mount it on the DR instances
Create a replication configuration from the eu-west-1 file system to a new file system in eu-central-1, and alarm on its TimeSinceLastSync metric

stem: An order service in us-east-1 sends custom events with PutEvents to a custom event bus named orders, whose rules start fulfillment workflows. The team deployed identical rules and targets in us-west-2 on a bus named orders-dr and now wants Regional fault tolerance for event ingestion. Requirements: events must flow to us-west-2 within 10 minutes after us-east-1 ingestion fails; traffic must return to us-east-1 automatically after recovery, with no manual health check reset; producers may add an endpoint ID to their PutEvents calls but take on no other changes. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Create Route 53 failover records that point a custom domain at the EventBridge API endpoints of both Regions, and point the producers at that domain
Create a custom event bus named orders in us-west-2, in the same account, with the DR rules, because global endpoints need matching bus names in both Regions
Add a rule on the us-east-1 orders bus that forwards every event to the us-west-2 bus, so the secondary Region already holds a copy of each event
Create the global endpoint with event replication turned off to avoid its extra cost, and rely on the Route 53 health check alone to move traffic back
Create an EventBridge global endpoint for the two buses with a Route 53 health check and event replication turned on, and have producers pass its endpoint ID

stem: A report API runs as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. Some report requests legitimately take up to 3 minutes. To speed up deployments, the team lowered the target group's deregistration delay to 30 seconds and set the container's stopTimeout to 120 seconds. The application keeps serving in-flight requests after it receives SIGTERM and exits when they finish. Since then, every rolling deployment cuts off some long report requests with 502 errors, while short requests never fail. Deployments may take longer, but no in-flight request may be lost. What should the team change?

choices.text: Raise the ECS service's health check grace period to 180 seconds, so the scheduler keeps old tasks registered until their long requests end
Raise the container's stopTimeout to 300 seconds, so the application has enough time after SIGTERM to finish every 3-minute report request
Raise the target group's deregistration delay to at least 180 seconds, because ECS waits for draining to finish before it sends the stop signal
Turn on slow start mode for the target group with a 180-second duration, so new tasks ramp up while the old tasks finish their long requests

stem: An order system runs on a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance. It must now survive the loss of an Availability Zone with automatic failover and no loss of committed transactions, and heavy reporting queries must move off the writer. A nightly job loads partner CSV files with the aws_s3 extension's table_import_from_s3 function and must keep running unchanged. Migrating to Aurora is out of scope this year. The team liked the typical under-35-second failover of a Multi-AZ DB cluster, but a failover of one to two minutes is acceptable. Which deployment meets these requirements?

choices.text: Convert to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and add a read replica in another Availability Zone that serves the reporting queries
Keep the Single-AZ primary, add two read replicas in other Availability Zones, and promote one with automation when the primary's zone fails
Convert to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and point the reporting queries at the standby instance's endpoint in the second Availability Zone
Move to a Multi-AZ DB cluster and send the reporting queries to its reader endpoint, which spreads them over the two readable standby instances

stem: An Aurora MySQL cluster, created two years ago with default settings, stores orders, invoices, and customers. At 10:05 a faulty release ran an UPDATE without a WHERE clause on the invoices table only; nobody noticed until 10:50. Orders and customers have received valid writes since then that must not be lost, and the cluster also feeds an external MySQL replica through binary log replication. The team must bring the invoices table back to its 10:04 state with minimal impact on the running application, which cannot be stopped during business hours. What should the team do?

choices.text: Backtrack the cluster to 10:04, then replay the orders and customers writes made after 10:05 from the binary logs onto the cluster
Modify the cluster to enable Backtrack with a 24-hour target window, then backtrack only the invoices table to its state at 10:04
Read the invoices rows from one of the cluster's Aurora Replicas, whose replica lag still holds the 10:04 version, and copy them back
Restore the cluster to a point in time of 10:04 as a new cluster, then copy the invoices rows from that cluster back into the production table

stem: Route 53 failover records for app.example.com are alias records pointing to an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1 (primary) and another in us-west-2 (secondary). The primary record is associated with an HTTPS health check created with the standard 30-second request interval and a failure threshold of 3. In a drill, new clients reached us-west-2 about 150 seconds after the primary stopped responding. The new target is under 90 seconds from failure until new clients resolve the secondary, and a single failed check must not trigger failover. What should the team do?

choices.text: Edit the existing health check's failure threshold to 1, so a 30-second check marks the primary unhealthy after a single failed response
Create a new health check with a 10-second request interval and a failure threshold of 2, and associate it with the primary failover record
Keep the existing health check, and set the TTL of both failover alias records to 10 seconds so that resolvers notice the change sooner
Edit the existing health check to use a 10-second request interval and a failure threshold of 2, and keep it associated with the primary record

stem: A standard accelerator in AWS Global Accelerator has two endpoint groups, us-east-1 and eu-west-1, each with one Application Load Balancer endpoint, and both traffic dials at 100 percent. Since Tuesday all traffic, including from US clients, has gone to eu-west-1, and the accelerator shows the us-east-1 endpoint as unhealthy. Yet the us-east-1 ALB's main /app/* target group has 12 healthy targets, and direct tests against the ALB succeed. On Tuesday a team stopped both instances of a /legacy-reports/* target group on that ALB, which a listener rule still uses. US users must return to us-east-1 while the legacy path stays offline. What should the team do?

choices.text: Remove the /legacy-reports/* listener rule and its target group from the us-east-1 ALB, so that every remaining target group has at least one healthy target
Raise the threshold count and shorten the interval in the us-east-1 endpoint group's Global Accelerator health check settings, so the ALB is rechecked faster
Change the /legacy-reports/* target group's success codes to 200-499, so its health checks pass while that path deliberately returns errors to users
Raise the us-east-1 ALB endpoint's weight to 255 in its endpoint group, so the accelerator prefers that endpoint even while it is reported as unhealthy

stem: A Lambda function with a 60-second timeout consumes a standard SQS queue (4-day retention) through an event source mapping with a 20-second batching window. The queue's visibility timeout is 60 seconds, and its redrive policy moves messages to a dead-letter queue after a maxReceiveCount of 1; the DLQ also keeps messages for 4 days. During bursts, some messages are processed twice, and messages land in the DLQ with no function error logged when Lambda is throttled. After weekend backlogs, messages can wait up to 2 days before their first receive, and operations needs 7 full days to review anything in the DLQ. Which THREE changes meet these needs? (Select THREE)

choices.text: Keep maxReceiveCount at 1 and turn on ReportBatchItemFailures, so only the messages that really failed return to the queue
Set the source queue's visibility timeout to 360 seconds, six times the function timeout with no batching allowance
Set the dead-letter queue's retention period to 7 days, the same length as the operations team's review window
Set the dead-letter queue's retention period to 14 days, longer than the source queue's 4-day retention period
Set the source queue's visibility timeout to 380 seconds, six times the function timeout plus the batching window
Set the redrive policy's maxReceiveCount to 5, so throttled batches get several chances before moving to the DLQ
